n: Around 734 BC, the kings of Syria (Aram) and northern Israel joined forces to attack Jerusalem, wanting to force Judah into their alliance against Assyria. This is called the Syro-Ephraimite War.

f.g: King of Aram (Syria), capital at Damascus.

n: When the royal family heard that Syria had allied with Israel, King Ahaz and his people trembled like trees shaking in the wind.

f.g: The leading tribe of the northern kingdom; a name for the whole kingdom of Israel.
Allied.

n: The Lord sends Isaiah to meet Ahaz at the water channel outside the city, where the king was likely inspecting Jerusalem’s water supply for the siege. Isaiah brings his son, whose name is itself a message.

f.g: “A remnant shall return” — a name of both warning and hope.
Where cloth was washed and bleached.

n: Isaiah tells Ahaz to stay calm and not fear these two kings, who are just smoldering stubs of firewood — almost burned out.

f.g: Charred sticks with only smoke left — enemies nearly finished.

n: Syria and Israel have plotted against Judah.

f.g: A wicked plan.

n: Their plan: invade Judah, break it open, and set up a puppet king, the son of Tabeal, in place of David’s line.

f.g: Terrify or harass.
An otherwise unknown man, likely an Aramean ally.

n: The Lord declares their plan will fail.

These kingdoms are led only by men — Damascus by Rezin. Within sixty-five years, Ephraim will be shattered as a people. Assyria conquered Samaria in 722 BC, and later resettlement completed Israel’s scattering.

f.g: Sixty-five years.

n: Samaria is led by Pekah, mere “Remaliah’s son.” Isaiah’s challenge to Ahaz: if you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all — a Hebrew wordplay.

f.w: If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established
f.g: Wordplay on the Hebrew root ’aman (believe/be firm): “No firm faith, no firm footing.”

n: The Lord speaks again to Ahaz through Isaiah.
God generously invites Ahaz to ask for any sign at all, as deep as the underworld or as high as heaven, to strengthen his faith.

f.w: in the depth, or in the height
f.g: Anything from the depths below to the heavens above.

n: Ahaz refuses, sounding pious: he won’t “test” God. But he had already decided to seek help from Assyria instead of trusting the Lord.

f.g: Test.

n: Isaiah rebukes the royal house: is it not enough to try the patience of people? Must they try God’s patience too?

f.g: The royal dynasty — the prophecy concerns David’s line.

n: So the Lord will give a sign Himself: a young woman — a virgin — will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, “God with us.” It had meaning in Ahaz’s day, and Matthew declares its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary.

f.g: Hebrew ‘almah — a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek Septuagint reads parthenos, “virgin.”
“God is with us.”

n: The child will eat curds and honey — simple food of a land returned to pasture — by the time he is old enough to know right from wrong.

f.g: Curds or thick yogurt.

n: Before the child is old enough to choose good over evil, the two kings Ahaz fears will be gone. Assyria killed Rezin around 732 BC, and Pekah was assassinated about the same time.
But because Ahaz trusted Assyria rather than God, the Lord will bring Assyria itself upon Judah — the worst days since the kingdom split after Solomon.
The Lord will whistle for Egypt’s armies like flies and Assyria’s like bees. Judah would be caught between these two superpowers.

f.g: Whistle or call.

n: These invaders will swarm everywhere — in valleys, rock crevices, thornbushes, and pastures. No place will be untouched.
The Lord will use Assyria, the “razor” Ahaz himself hired, to shave Judah completely — head, beard, and body. Shaving a man was a deep humiliation.

f.g: Ahaz paid Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:8); now that hired razor will turn on Judah.
East of the Euphrates — Assyria.

n: So few people will be left that a man will keep only one young cow and two sheep.
With so few people, the animals will give plenty of milk, and survivors will live on curds and wild honey — the simple diet of an empty land.
Rich vineyards worth a fortune will be overgrown with briers and thorns.

f.g: Shekels of silver — a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels.

n: The land will become so wild that people will go there only to hunt with bows and arrows.
Even hillsides once carefully hoed will become pasture for cattle and sheep because no one will farm them.

f.g: A digging tool like a hoe or pickaxe.
Sheep and goats.
